 WHO urges countries to accelerate action on national priority lists to improve access to assistive technology
 WHO urges countries to accelerate action on national priority lists to improve access to assistive technology
 19 November 2026 
 News release 
 Bangkok, Thailand 
 Reading time: 
 The World Health Organization today called on countries in the South-East Asia Region to accelerate efforts to improve access to assistive technology by developing and implementing national Priority Assistive Products Lists (APLs), supported by adequate financing, sustainable procurement, stronger service delivery and support system for the entire life-cycle of assistive products.
 More than 2.5 billion people worldwide need one or more assistive products, such as wheelchairs, hearing aids, spectacles, prostheses and communication aids. This number is expected to rise to 3.5 billion by 2050, driven by ageing population and increasing prevalence of noncommunicable diseases. Yet nearly one billion people are unable to access the products they need, limiting their independence and participation in society, while many more have to incur out of pocket spending to access the assistive products.
 “Assistive technology must be an integral part of health systems. Developing national priority lists is an important step, but countries must also ensure that these products are financed, procured and delivered through accessible services. This requires sustained investment and coordinated action across sectors to ensure that people who need assistive products are not left behind,” said Dr Nilesh Buddha, Officer-in-Charge, WHO South-East Asia Region.
 High costs, limited availability, inadequate services and shortages of trained personnel continue to prevent many people, particularly in underserved communities, from accessing and using appropriate assistive products.
 In 2018, the World Health Assembly called on Member States to strengthen policies and programmes to improve access to assistive technology. In September this year, the WHO Regional Committee for South-East Asia also reaffirmed the importance of equitable access to quality-assured and affordable medical devices, including assistive technologies, calling for stronger national systems.
 A national Priority Assistive Products List (APL) helps countries identify products that should be made available as a priority, based on population needs, available evidence and national capacities. The WHO model APL, updated in 2026, includes 66 categories of assistive products and provides a reference for countries to develop lists suited to their national contexts.
 Countries in the Region are making progress. With WHO support, Bhutan, India. Nepal  and Timor-Leste have developed or revised and adopted national APLs. Bangladesh has developed a draft list and an investment case, while WHO has supported the development of a national list in Maldives. Additionally, in India, WHO supported rapid assessments of assistive technology needs and a WHO–ICMR roundtable that helped establish assistive technology as a national health research priority. In Nepal, WHO supported training of health professionals to strengthen service delivery.
 However, developing a list is only the first step. Countries need to integrate priority products into national health plans, budgets and universal health coverage benefit packages, and ensure their availability through primary health care and other appropriate services. A life-cycle approach, covering procurement, training, maintenance and timely replacement, is essential to ensure that products remain safe and functional.
 To support these efforts, WHO and the Sirindhorn National Medical Rehabilitation Institute (SNMRI) have convened the two-day multi-country technical workshop that began here this morning, bringing together representatives from eight countries in the Region, alongside technical experts and development partners.  The participants are exploring how to adapt the WHO model list to national needs, engage relevant stakeholders, identify priority products and develop country roadmaps for implementation.
 WHO has been advocating for Member States to prioritize assistive technology in national health agendas; develop and implement evidence-informed national APLs; involve persons with disabilities and people who use assistive products in decision-making; and integrate priority products into national budgets and universal health coverage benefit packages, supported by stronger procurement, maintenance and service delivery systems.
 “Expanding access to assistive technology is essential to advancing universal health coverage and reducing inequalities. Sustained national action is needed to ensure that everyone who needs assistive products can access and use them, regardless of where they live or their ability to pay,” Dr Buddha said.
